transcript:
Interviewer: Can you walk me through a time you had to make a hard product decision with incomplete data?

Candidate: Sure. At my last company we were six weeks from launch on a payments feature and discovered our fraud detection model was flagging 12% of legitimate transactions — way above the 2% threshold we'd set. Engineering estimated a full fix would take eight weeks. I pulled together a quick data analysis, mapped the user segments most affected, and proposed a tiered rollout: launch to low-risk segments first, cap exposure to roughly 20% of volume, and set a hard kill switch if flags exceeded 5%. I aligned the CEO and head of Risk in a thirty-minute meeting, then ran a week-long pilot before full launch. We hit 1.8% false positives by week four.

Interviewer: How did you handle pushback from the engineering lead who wanted to delay the full launch?

Candidate: He had a fair point — shipping with a known defect felt wrong. I didn't dismiss it. I acknowledged the risk directly in the document, quantified the cost of delay in terms of revenue and competitive timing, and offered him a named escalation path if the kill-switch threshold was ever crossed. That gave him a credible fallback. He signed off.

Interviewer: Tell me about a project that failed and what you learned.

Candidate: We launched an in-app coaching feature that saw 40% drop-off after day three. In retrospect I had prioritized the feature roadmap over the activation funnel. I had data showing low activation but convinced myself it was a content problem, not a flow problem. It was both. I now require a user journey walkthrough before any feature gets a green-light, regardless of how confident I am in the concept.

Interviewer: How do you communicate product strategy to an engineering team that's skeptical of PM-led decisions?

Candidate: I start by asking them what questions they'd want answered before they'd trust the direction. That surfaces real concerns, not just surface-level skepticism. Then I bring the evidence — user research, data, competitive context — and I make the trade-offs visible, not buried. I try to never surprise them with a decision; I'd rather over-communicate during the problem-framing phase and have shorter alignment conversations at decision time.

dimensions.name: Problem Solving
dimensions.description: Structures ambiguous problems, synthesizes data, and reaches sound decisions under uncertainty.

anchors.definition: Struggles to frame the problem; relies on others to structure thinking.
Identifies the problem but analysis is shallow or incomplete.
Breaks down complex problems clearly; uses data and judgment well.
Exceptional rigor; anticipates second-order effects; reframes problems to surface better solutions.

dimensions.name: Execution
dimensions.description: Drives work from ambiguity to outcome; manages risk, scope, and stakeholders through delivery.

anchors.definition: Work frequently stalls; poor follow-through or accountability.
Delivers on defined tasks but struggles with ambiguity or cross-functional coordination.
Reliable delivery; proactively manages blockers and communicates trade-offs.
Creates momentum in ambiguous environments; builds systems that scale beyond themselves.

dimensions.name: Communication
dimensions.description: Adapts message to audience; drives alignment and trust through clarity and transparency.

anchors.definition: Communicates adequately but misses audience calibration or leaves gaps.
Clear, audience-aware; proactively shares context and surfaces disagreement.
Creates clarity in ambiguous situations; builds trust even with skeptics.
